segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Good morning, everyone.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: I've been invited to talk about my research project into Australian Aboriginal rock paintings.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: The Australian Aborigines have recorded both real and symbolic images of their time on rock walls for many thousands of years.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Throughout the long history of this tradition, new images have appeared and new painting styles have developed.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: And these characteristics can be used to categorise the different artistic styles.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Among these are what we call the Dynamic, Yam and Modern styles of painting.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: One of the most significant characteristics of the different styles is the way that humans are depicted in the paintings.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: The more recent paintings show people in static poses.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: But the first human images to dominate rock art paintings, over 8,000 years ago, were full of movement.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: These paintings showed people hunting and cooking food and so they were given the name 'Dynamic' to reflect this energy.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: It's quite amazing considering they were painted in such a simple stick-like form.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: In the Yam period, there was a movement away from stick figures to a more naturalistic shape.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: However, they didn't go as far as the Modern style, which is known as 'x-ray' because it actually makes a feature of the internal skeleton as well as the organs of animals and humans.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: The Yam style of painting got its name from the fact that it featured much curvier figures that actually resemble the vegetable called a yam, which is similar to a sweet potato.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: The Mode~n paintings are interesting because they include paintings at the time of the first contact with European settlers.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Aborigines managed to convey the idea of the settlers' clothing by simply painting the Europeans without any hands, indicating the habit of standing with their hands in their pockets!

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Size is another charncteristic.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: The more recent images tend to be life size or even larger, but the Dynamic figures are painted in miniature.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Aboriginal rock art also records the environmental changes that occurred over thousands of years.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: For , we know from the Dynamic paintings that over 8,000 years ago, Aborigines would have rarely eaten fish and sea levels were much lower at this time.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: In fact, fish didn't start to appear in paintings until the Yam period along with shells and other marine images.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: The paintings of the Yam tradition also suggest that, during this time, the Aborigines moved away from animals as their main food source and began including vegetables in their diet, as these feature prominently.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Freshwater creatures didn't appear in the paintings until the Modern period from 4,000 years ago.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: So, these paintings have already taught us a lot.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: But one image that has always intrigued us is known as the 'Rainbow Serpent'.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: The Rainbow Serpent, which is the focus of my most recent project, gets its name from its snake or serpent-likebody and it first appeared in the Yam period 4 to 6,000 years ago.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Many believe it is a curious mixture of kangaroo, snake and crocodile.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: But we decided to study the Rainbow Serpent paintingsto see if we could locate the animal that the very first painters based their image on.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: The Yam period coincided with the end of the last ice age.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: This broughtabout tremendous change in the environment,with the sea levels rising and creepingsteadily inland.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: This flooded many familiar land features and also caused a great deal of disruptionto traditional patterns of life, hunting in particular.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: New shores were formed and totally different creatures would have washed up onto the shores.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: We studied 107 paintingsof the Rainbow Serpent and found that the one creature that matches it most closely was the RibbonedPipefish, which is a type of sea horse.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: This sea creaturewould have been a totally unfamiliar sight in the inland regions where the image is found and may have been the inspiration behind the early paintings.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: So, at the end of the ice age there would have been enormous changesin animal and plant life.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: It's not surprising then, that the Aborigines linked this abundanceto the new creatures they witnessed.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Even today, Aborigines see the Rainbow Serpent as a symbol of creation, which is understandablegiven the increase in vegetation and the new life forms that featured when the image first appeared.
